items.stem: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain why it allows us to use thermometers.
items.answer: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other; the thermometer is C, so equal readings mean equal temperatures.

items.stem: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa from 4 L to 5 L. How much work does it do?

items.markingKey: W = area under the line (trapezium) = ½(P₁ + P₂)(V₂ − V₁) = ½(1 + 2) × 10⁵ × 4 × 10⁻³ = 600 J.

items.stem: A gas is supplied 1000 J of heat and does 300 J of work on its surroundings. Find the change in its internal energy.
items.markingKey: First law: ΔU = Q − W, where W is the work done BY the gas = 1000 − (300) = 700 J.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about heat, work and internal energy is correct?

items.stem: Why do we say that a body has internal energy but not "heat content"?
items.answer: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference; once transferred it becomes part of internal energy, which is a state variable.

items.stem: Explain why the work done by a gas depends on the path taken between two states.
items.answer: Work is the area under the P-V curve, which differs for different paths between the same end points.

items.answer: W = −100 J (net work done on the gas 100 J); Q = −100 J; ΔU = 0

items.stem: Air (γ = 1.4) at 1 × 10⁵ Pa is compressed to 1/3 of its volume (i) isothermally and (ii) adiabatically. Find the final pressure in each case and explain why they differ.
items.markingKey: (i) PV = const ⇒ P₂ = 3P₁ = 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa (1). (ii) PV^γ = const ⇒ P₂ = P₁ × 3^1.4 = 4.66 × 10⁵ Pa (1). Adiabatic compression also raises the temperature, giving a higher pressure (1).
